part_title: Amazon EKS: Kubernetes Control Plane, GenAI Architecture, Nodes and Storage

scenes.title: Amazon EKS overview
scenes.narration: Begin with the managed Kubernetes control plane shown at the top. Amazon EKS operates components such as the Kubernetes API server and critical scheduling and control functions. Developers and CI/CD systems submit desired state through supported Kubernetes APIs. Beneath that are the worker environments where containers actually run, commonly EC2 worker nodes or supported Fargate pods. Kubernetes Deployments describe desired replicas and rollout behavior, Pods are the scheduling units that contain application containers, and Services give stable access to selected Pods. This separation is important: AWS operating the control plane does not mean AWS automatically handles every workload configuration or worker-node security. For EC2-backed nodes, patching, capacity and storage choices still matter according to the node-management model. For an API deployment, use a readiness probe to determine whether a Pod is prepared to receive traffic, and distinguish that from a liveness probe intended to detect a process that needs restarting. Use EKS when Kubernetes portability, controllers, policy integration or operating patterns justify the added complexity.

scenes.title: EKS architecture for a GenAI service
scenes.narration: This architecture starts with users entering through an Application Load Balancer and a Kubernetes Service that routes traffic to GenAI application Pods. The Pods run inside a dedicated namespace. From there, application logic invokes Bedrock for model inference, accesses RDS for conversations or other structured metadata, reads S3 for approved documents, and queries OpenSearch for semantic retrieval. Separate ingestion Pods prepare and index source content for retrieval. The security arrow beneath the application highlights IAM roles for service accounts, or IRSA. It lets appropriately configured Pods obtain AWS credentials tied to a Kubernetes service account instead of shipping access keys inside the container. On compatible EKS configurations, Pod Identity is another option that should be evaluated separately. Each Pod should receive only the Bedrock, S3, RDS or search permissions its function needs. Private routing, data-access controls and TLS still matter even when a Pod has an IAM role. This is a layered RAG system: ingress, orchestration, model access, structured data and vector retrieval have different operational and security responsibilities.

scenes.title: EKS node types
scenes.narration: The slide compares three worker-capacity models. Managed node groups provide an EC2-backed option where EKS automates supported node provisioning, lifecycle and updates, while you still choose instance families, scaling configuration and workloads. Self-managed nodes give your team finer control over the EC2 lifecycle, custom AMIs and special configurations, but also more patching and scaling responsibility. Fargate profiles schedule eligible Pods onto managed compute so you don't directly administer EC2 worker nodes. Look at the workload guidance: standard microservices usually fit managed node groups, specialised GPU or host-level agents may need EC2 nodes, and appropriately supported lightweight workloads may fit Fargate. Not every Kubernetes capability and storage or daemon workload is supported identically on Fargate. For GenAI inference, GPU availability, model memory, custom device plugins and startup time may make an EC2-backed configuration necessary. Selection should follow the actual Pod requirements, node security posture, networking design and cost profile, not simply the promise of least administration.

scenes.title: EKS Persistent Storage
scenes.narration: Here the left half shows EBS block storage provisioned for a Kubernetes Pod through a PersistentVolumeClaim. That volume is tied to an Availability Zone, so the scheduler must place the Pod where the volume can attach. EBS is useful for low-latency block storage serving a stateful application, and you need the supported EBS CSI driver and appropriate StorageClass. The right half shows Amazon EFS as a regional shared file system, which can be mounted by multiple Pods across Availability Zones using an EFS CSI driver and supported access modes such as ReadWriteMany. The diagram emphasises the choice between a single-AZ block device and shared multi-AZ file access. Don't infer that an EBS-backed Pod becomes multi-AZ resilient just because Kubernetes reschedules it; the storage attachment and recovery strategy must be designed. Similarly, EFS sharing doesn't automatically fix application-level concurrent-write problems. Choose storage based on persistence needs, access pattern, consistency expectations, performance and required recovery behavior.
